The scene contract: what vellumplot and vellumwidget depend on

Source: vignettes/scene-contract.Rmd
scene-contract.Rmd

vellum is the backend for a small ecosystem: vellumplot compiles a grammar of graphics into a vellum scene, and vellumwidget turns a rendered scene into an interactive HTML widget. Both bind to a narrow seam: scene_model(), scene_svg(), and the per-element metadata that rides on grobs. Above the SVG-comfortable element count a host switches to a rasterised base layer, and takes those pixels from scene_png() (raw bytes, no temp file) — part of the same seam. Because the three packages are version-locked and co-released, a change to that seam can break the layers above it silently.

This article is the authoritative description of that seam. If you are building on vellum, or changing vellum’s output, this is the contract to hold to. (It supersedes the internal design note _docs/DESIGN-INTERACTIVITY.md, which is kept only as history.)

The seam, in one picture 

  vellumplot  ──compiles a plot to grobs carrying──▶  key / meta / id / role
                                                        │
  vellum  ──renders──▶  scene_svg()   (data-key, data-vellum-*, role attrs)
                        scene_model()  (per-element table: identity + bbox)
                        scene_png()    (raw PNG bytes, for the raster-base mode)
                                                        │
  vellumwidget  ──reads scene_svg() + scene_model()──▶  hover / select / brush / link

Everything below the grammar is pure metadata: a static PNG/SVG render never calls scene_model(), and a grob without a key/meta still draws exactly as before. Nothing here changes what is painted.

Carrying identity on a grob

Eleven constructors take two optional identity arguments: the batched marks points_grob(), circle_grob(), rect_grob(), segments_grob(), hexagon_grob(), sector_grob(), roundrect_grob() and text_grob(), and the single-shape marks lines_grob(), polygon_grob() and path_grob().

  • key: a character vector of data keys. This is the join key a host uses to tie an on-screen element back to a datum.
  • meta: a list of free-form per-element records, e.g. a tooltip string or field values. It can also be given columnar: a data frame with one row per element and one column per field. Row i stands for the record of that row’s values (a NULL entry in a list-column leaves its field out of the record), and it costs far less than a list of records when there are many elements.

On a batched mark both are per element and must have length 1 (shared by every element) or exactly the element count; any other length is an error naming the argument, never a silent truncation or wrap. A single-shape mark is one element, so it takes a single key and a single meta record.

Every grob also takes id and role (a single value per grob) for semantic identity and accessibility. The remaining constructors (bezier_grob(), spline_grob(), loop_grob(), raster_grob(), svg_grob(), text_path_grob(), contour_grob()) take no key and never appear in the tables below.

Coordinates: bare numbers are npc

A bare number passed to any constructor’s position or size argument is read in default_units, which is "npc" (a fraction of the enclosing viewport) everywhere, as in grid. A grammar layer placing data values inside a panel viewport with an xscale/yscale must therefore say so, either with vl_unit(x, "native") or default_units = "native":

panel <- vl_scene(3, 2, bg = "white") |>
  push(vl_viewport(name = "panel", xscale = c(0, 10), yscale = c(0, 100))) |>
  draw(points_grob(
    x = c(2, 5, 8),
    y = c(20, 80, 50),
    default_units = "native",
    key = c("a", "b", "c")
  )) |>
  pop()
panel

Arguments with a physical default keep it whatever default_units says: a bare point, hexagon or loop size, foot, start_cap, end_cap and offset are millimetres. Only the reading of bare numbers changes; a [vl_unit()] is never reinterpreted.

s <- vl_scene(5, 3, bg = "white") |>
  draw(points_grob(
    x    = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75),
    y    = c(0.4, 0.7, 0.4),
    size = vl_unit(6, "mm"),
    gp   = vl_gpar(fill = "#3498db", col = NA),
    key  = c("a", "b", "c"),
    meta = list(
      list(tooltip = "first"),
      list(tooltip = "second"),
      list(tooltip = "third")
    )
  ))
s

(Each batched grob carries one graphical style; the grammar layer above vellum emits one grob per style bucket, so a scatter with three colours is three points_grob()s. The key/meta machinery is per element regardless.)

scene_model(): the per-element table

scene_model() walks the rendered scene and returns a list of two data frames.

m <- scene_model(s)
names(m)
#> [1] "elements" "panels"

elements

One row per drawn element of the keyable marks, in paint order:

str(m$elements)
#> 'data.frame':    3 obs. of  14 variables:
#>  $ key  : chr  "a" "b" "c"
#>  $ mark : chr  "point" "point" "point"
#>  $ id   : chr  NA NA NA
#>  $ name : chr  NA NA NA
#>  $ panel: chr  NA NA NA
#>  $ x0   : num  97.3 217.3 337.3
#>  $ y0   : num  150.1 63.7 150.1
#>  $ x1   : num  143 263 383
#>  $ y1   : num  195 109 195
#>  $ x    : num  120 240 360
#>  $ y    : num  172.8 86.4 172.8
#>  $ w    : num  45.4 45.4 45.4
#>  $ h    : num  45.4 45.4 45.4
#>  $ meta :List of 3
#>   ..$ :List of 1
#>   .. ..$ tooltip: chr "first"
#>   ..$ :List of 1
#>   .. ..$ tooltip: chr "second"
#>   ..$ :List of 1
#>   .. ..$ tooltip: chr "third"

The columns are the contract:

column type meaning
key character the data key (NA if the element was drawn without one)
mark character the mark kind (see vocabulary below)
id character the grob id (NA if unset)
name character the grob name (NA if unset)
panel character the innermost enclosing named viewport (NA if none)
x0, y0, x1, y1 numeric device-pixel bounding box
x, y numeric element centre, (x0+x1)/2, (y0+y1)/2
w, h numeric element size, x1-x0, y1-y0
meta list the free-form per-element record (list-column; see below for the columnar form)

scene_model(scene, meta = "columns") returns the same table with meta as a data-frame column instead: one row per element and one column per field. A field is a plain vector when every element carrying it holds one atomic value of one type (NA for the elements without it), and a list-column (NULL where absent) otherwise. A host that reads meta for many elements (vellumwidget does) asks for this form, so no per-element record is ever built.

scene_model(s, meta = "columns")$elements$meta
#>   tooltip
#> 1   first
#> 2  second
#> 3   third

The mark vocabulary is these eleven values, and only these: rect, point, circle, hexagon, sector, segment, roundrect, text, path, line, polygon. Adding one is a contract change (see the end of this article).

Three families produce these rows:

  • Batched marks (rect, point, circle, hexagon, sector, segment) emit one row per element, always, even when unkeyed (then key is NA).
  • Keyed-only batches (roundrect, text) emit one row per keyed element. A grob drawn without key contributes no rows at all, and within a keyed grob an element whose key is NA or "" is skipped. This keeps a plot’s unkeyed axis labels and strip backgrounds out of the table.
  • Single-shape marks (path, line, polygon) emit one row per grob, and only when keyed. An unkeyed path/line/polygon is geometry-only and does not appear in the table. (A single sf feature, one polygon or linestring, is exactly one such element.) Key one with the constructor’s key argument (setting the grob’s @keys slot is equivalent).

panels

One row per named panel that encloses at least one row of elements (a named viewport becomes an addressable panel; one with no elements in the table has no row). An element’s panel is its innermost enclosing named viewport.

str(m$panels)
#> 'data.frame':    0 obs. of  14 variables:
#>  $ name     : chr 
#>  $ x0       : num 
#>  $ y0       : num 
#>  $ x1       : num 
#>  $ y1       : num 
#>  $ px0      : num 
#>  $ py0      : num 
#>  $ px1      : num 
#>  $ py1      : num 
#>  $ xscale_lo: num 
#>  $ xscale_hi: num 
#>  $ yscale_lo: num 
#>  $ yscale_hi: num 
#>  $ meta     : list()

Columns:

column type meaning
name character the panel’s viewport name
x0, y0, x1, y1 numeric bounding box of the panel’s elements (device px)
px0, py0, px1, py1 numeric the panel viewport’s resolved device-px rectangle — the true data region, from the layout solve, not just where marks landed (NA if the viewport was not captured)
xscale_lo, xscale_hi numeric the panel viewport’s native x coordinate range (its xscale)
yscale_lo, yscale_hi numeric native y coordinate range (its yscale)
meta list the panel viewport’s free-form meta (list-column; NULL when none)

The pixel rectangle paired with the native range gives the affine that maps device px ↔︎ native for that panel — the geometry a host needs to invert a pixel back to a data coordinate. It is the panel-level analogue of an element’s bbox + meta.

The panel-level meta (the meta = argument of [vl_viewport()]) is the same opaque, host-read channel as element meta: vellum carries it untouched and names no conventions. The grammar uses it for panel-scoped descriptors — e.g. the scales descriptor vellumplot attaches to each data panel (per-axis type, domain, breaks, and labels), which vellumwidget reads to map pixels back to data values. That convention is documented by vellumplot, not here.

The meta key vocabulary

vellum treats meta as opaque: it is a free-form list, recycled to the element count and carried through untouched; vellum does not name or validate its keys. The following key names are conventions the grammar (vellumplot) writes and the widget (vellumwidget) reads. Documenting them here keeps the three layers in step; they are not enforced by vellum.

meta key written by read by purpose
tooltip vellumplot tooltip= vellumwidget hover tooltip text (falls back to key)
data_id vellumplot data_id= (becomes the key) the data key for an element
hover_group vellumplot hover_group= vellumwidget co-highlight a group on hover
hover_color vellumplot mark aesthetic vellumwidget per-element hover outline colour
selected_color vellumplot mark aesthetic vellumwidget per-element selection colour
legend vellumplot legend keying vellumwidget the series a mark belongs to
legend_for vellumplot legend keying vellumwidget the series a legend swatch drives ("<aes>:<level>")

If you add a convention, add it here.

element_geometry(): the hit-test geometry

scene_model() gives boxes, which suit a rectangular brush and mislead for anything diagonal, thin or holed. A host that hit-tests on the client (a browser cannot call back into R on every mouse move) reads element_geometry() once instead: the device-pixel geometry of every keyed element, recorded by the same walk that renders the scene, so a segment drawn with an offset or end caps is reported where it lands. vl_nearest() measures against exactly this geometry, so a client that follows the rules below reproduces it.

holed <- vl_scene(4, 3, dpi = 100) |>
  draw(path_grob(
    x = c(0.1, 0.9, 0.9, 0.1, 0.4, 0.6, 0.6, 0.4),
    y = c(0.1, 0.1, 0.9, 0.9, 0.4, 0.4, 0.6, 0.6),
    id = rep(1:2, each = 4),
    rule = "evenodd",
    key = "donut"
  ))
element_geometry(holed)
#>     key kind vertex ring   x   y    rule
#> 1 donut path      1    1  40 270 evenodd
#> 2 donut path      2    1 360 270 evenodd
#> 3 donut path      3    1 360  30 evenodd
#> 4 donut path      4    1  40  30 evenodd
#> 5 donut path      5    2 160 180 evenodd
#> 6 donut path      6    2 240 180 evenodd
#> 7 donut path      7    2 240 120 evenodd
#> 8 donut path      8    2 160 120 evenodd

One row per vertex. The columns are the contract:

column type meaning
key character the element’s data key (repeated on each of its vertices)
kind character segment, line, polygon, path, hexagon, sector, point, rect, roundrect, text (a circle_grob() element reports as point)
vertex integer 1-based within the element; restarts at 1 for the next element
ring integer 1-based ring (or polyline) within the element
x, y numeric device px, y down
rule character the fill rule, per element: "nonzero", "evenodd", or NA for a kind with no interior (segment, line, point)

The rules a client applies, which are the ones vl_nearest() applies:

  • segment and line are open centre-lines: the distance is to the nearest edge, and an NA vertex is a break.
  • point is a single centre; its radius is half the smaller side of its scene_model() box.
  • rect and roundrect are two opposite box corners, filled as "nonzero".
  • Everything else (polygon, path, hexagon, sector, and a text label’s box) is closed rings. Containment is decided once, across all of an element’s rings, under its rule: even-odd parity of the edge crossings, or a nonzero sum of the rings’ winding numbers. Inside is distance zero. Outside – and a point in a hole is outside – the distance is to the nearest edge of any ring. Rings are never joined: each closes on itself.

rule comes from the grob: path_grob(rule = "evenodd") reports "evenodd", and rule = "winding" (the default) and every other filled kind report "nonzero". vl_nearest() and hit_test() both decide containment by that rule, so a click in the hole of an even-odd path is outside it, and hit_test() falls through to whatever is drawn beneath:

vl_nearest(holed, 0.5, 0.5)$dist # in the hole: outside, so a positive distance
#> [1] 30
vl_nearest(holed, 0.2, 0.5)$dist # in the ring: inside
#> [1] 0
is.null(hit_test(holed, 0.5, 0.5)) # nothing under the hole
#> [1] TRUE

scene_svg(): the emitted attributes

scene_svg() returns the same scene as an SVG string. Interactivity rides on SVG attributes; the raster and PDF backends ignore all of them.

svg <- scene_svg(s)
# the data-key attributes on the three points:
regmatches(svg, gregexpr('data-key="[^"]*"', svg))[[1]]
#> [1] "data-key=\"a\"" "data-key=\"b\"" "data-key=\"c\""

Six attributes, each emitted only when its source is set:

attribute source scope set from
data-key grob key per element points_grob(key=) etc. (every constructor that takes key)
data-vellum-id grob id per grob/node *_grob(id=)
data-vellum-name grob name per grob/node *_grob(name=)
role grob role per grob/node *_grob(role=)
data-vellum-panel named viewport wrapping <g> vl_viewport(name=)
data-vellum-pan pannable panel’s inner group inner <g> vl_viewport(pannable=)

An empty/NULL source emits no attribute, so a scene that declares no interactivity is byte-for-byte identical to one built before any of this existed.

Pannable panels

A named viewport marked vl_viewport(pannable = TRUE) is emitted as two nested groups instead of one: an outer <g data-vellum-panel="name"> that carries the panel’s clip (untransformed, so the clip region stays fixed) around an inner <g data-vellum-pan="name"> holding the content. The panel’s clip is hoisted once to the outer group (rather than repeated per element), so a host can set a transform on the inner group to pan/zoom the marks while the clip — and the axes/legend outside the panel — stay put. This is the structural basis for host-side axis-aware zoom. It is SVG-only and inert for static rendering (the extra group has no transform until a host sets one); non-pannable panels and other backends are unchanged.

Accessibility

A scene carries an optional accessible name and description, set with vl_scene(title=, desc=) or describe(scene, title=, desc=). When present:

  • the SVG root becomes <svg role="img" aria-labelledby="…"> with <title> and <desc> children (the reliable screen-reader pattern; WCAG 1.1.1);
  • the PDF is a tagged PDF: the chart is a Figure in the structure tree whose Alt is the description.

This is additive: with no title/desc the output is unchanged. The grammar layer (vellumplot) sets these automatically from the plot’s title and an auto-generated (or labs(alt=)) alt text. See vellumplot’s Accessibility article. Per-element role (above) is a genuine ARIA role; the interactive widget layer (vellumwidget) adds keyboard navigation and live-region announcements on top.

Invariants the contract guarantees

These are the properties vellumplot and vellumwidget are entitled to rely on, and that vellum’s own tests (tests/testthat/test-contract.R) pin down:

  1. Paint order. scene_model()$elements is in draw order, and the SVG emits elements in the same order. A host can zip the SVG DOM and the table positionally.
  2. Semantic/geometry agreement. scene_model() builds the identity columns from the R grob tree and the geometry columns from the compiled backend, then asserts they enumerate the same elements: the element counts must match and the key column must be identical at every position. A mismatch is a hard error (a compiler bug), never a silent mis-join.
  3. Additivity. key/meta/id/role never change what is drawn. A render with no keys is identical to the same scene without the machinery, on every backend.
  4. Stable id join key. A grob’s id surfaces as data-vellum-id in the SVG and is the join key vellumplot records in its provenance table, so a widget can map an SVG node to the grammar record that produced it.

For contributors

If you change any of the following, update this article and the contract tests in the same commit, and expect to co-release vellumplot and vellumwidget:

  • the elements/panels column set or types,
  • the element_geometry() column set, its kind and rule vocabularies, or the containment rule above,
  • the mark vocabulary,
  • which marks are keyable, or the batched / keyed-only / single-shape rules,
  • the key/meta length rule (1 or the element count),
  • the default reading of bare numbers (default_units = "npc"),
  • the SVG attribute names, or when they are emitted,
  • the reserved meta key vocabulary. ```
